text:
I want to begin with the broader puzzle rather than with the framework term itself.
Today, AI is entering more real decision settings, including crisis judgment, organizational governance, public administration, healthcare, and other high-risk contexts.
That means AI is no longer only a laboratory system or a stand-alone tool. It is increasingly embedded in real organizational and institutional decision chains.
So the opening question is how that broader shift changes human judgment once AI becomes part of the process.

text:
Existing research usually approaches AI in decision-making from three familiar questions.
The first is whether AI improves judgment quality or performance.
The second is whether people trust, adopt, or rely on AI advice.
The third is how responsibility should be assigned once AI is involved in decision-making.
These questions are important, but they still tend to treat AI as an external tool.

This is where the gap becomes visible.
We do have important literatures on judgment quality, on trust and reliance, and on responsibility after AI-assisted outcomes.
But these streams are usually treated separately.
What remains underexplained is the process itself: how belief formation, reliance calibration, and responsibility attribution unfold inside one connected decision process.

text:
This matters because people increasingly use AI in a different way from traditional tools.
They do not use it only as a search engine, calculator, or automation device.
They consult it, discuss with it, confirm with it, and sometimes rely on it as a source of judgment.
In these interactions, AI is not simply giving an answer. It also shapes how users understand the problem itself.

text:
This change is closely related to the technical foundation and interaction form of large language models.
LLMs are not simply larger versions of traditional algorithms.
Their Transformer architecture supports contextual integration, and later tuning makes them able to explain, respond, and interact continuously with users.
So the difference is not only output accuracy. The form of output and the mode of interaction also change.
That is why users can be influenced by explanation, tone, and narrative framing, not only by the answer itself.

In this sense, the impact of AI should not be understood only as whether people adopt AI advice.
It should be understood as how AI reorganizes the decision-making process itself.
AI can change how information is presented, how cognitive burden is distributed, how action thresholds are adjusted, and how responsibility is understood after action.
That is why I treat belief formation, reliance calibration, and responsibility attribution as linked stages of one AI-mediated decision process.

text:
The dissertation then narrows that broader problem into a more specific theoretical object: AI as decision architecture.
I use this as an integrative analytical framework, not as a claim that the theory is already fully settled.
The framework highlights four things AI can restructure: information flow, cognitive burden, action thresholds, and responsibility relations.
In other words, AI matters not only because it produces content, but because it reorganizes how consequential human decisions are reached.

text:
This is where the three papers fit together.
Paper 1 studies the mapping from evidence to belief.
Paper 2 studies how belief and feedback recalibrate action thresholds and reliance under repeated interaction.
Paper 3 studies how action connects to responsibility attribution once AI-assisted outcomes occur.
This also explains why I begin with Paper 1.
If the evidence-to-belief mapping is already reshaped by answer-first AI, later reliance and responsibility are built on that altered base.
So the first paper is the natural starting point for the dissertation's empirical analysis.
